title: Maui Mayoral Candidates Forum: Housing, Bill 9 & Lahaina Recovery

recap.headline: Kīhei Community Association holds forum for Maui County mayor candidates
recap.in_60_seconds: The Kīhei Community Association held this forum for Maui County mayor candidates at ProArts, before the August 8 primary. Nine of the 10 mayoral candidates took part. Candidates drew numbers for order and each gave an opening statement of about two minutes, then answered questions in three groups of three with about two minutes per answer. There were no audience questions. Questions covered housing affordability, why each wants to be mayor, traffic, flooding, Bill 9, water supply, county reform, houselessness, evacuation routes, reef pollution and a highway crossing near a high school.
recap.moderated_by: Kīhei Community Association moderators, led by the association's president

answers.summary: Said he has worked since childhood, ran a restaurant kitchen at 16 and became chef of a Michigan golf resort at 24. Said that with Hungry Heroes Hawaiʻi he helped give 350,000 meals before the fires and $10,000 of produce twice a week to survivors for two years. Wants accountability, a close look at the budget and small community wins before bigger projects.

Said he is running reluctantly because, as a Hawaiian, he sees genocidal crimes and illegal occupation in Hawaiʻi for more than 130 years. Said denationalization forces people to become American, and elected officials have been put on notice. Said he wants to represent the Hawaiian Kingdom and that the fire was not a wildfire.

Said she is studying for a medical coding license and is running because she believes real change is possible. Said owning a home has been out of reach for 40 years and most residents cannot afford homes or groceries. Proposed rent control and taxing owners of homes or property worth over $5 million.

Said he wants to be the voice of the people and that capitalism leads to greed and corruption. Proposed cutting the mayor's salary by 75%, leaving about 4,400 a month. Said he has a little over a thousand now, works with a rescue mission doing showers, and has worked where people have no water or electricity.

Said she is in her 10th year on the Maui County Council and has worked for Governor Ariyoshi, Senator Akaka and Senator Hirono. Said her son in Chicago cannot afford to come home and she wants to increase housing and affordability. Proposed a permitting office in the mayor's office and using R-1 water in Kīhei for green waste and reef protection.

Said he is a former NASA engineer focused on wastewater since 1983. Said millions of gallons a day of wastewater go into the ocean on the North Shore and South Shore without pathogen treatment, and he cannot get $900,000 for North Shore disinfection while $140 million goes to enforcement. Proposed a Maui Living ʻĀina Stabilization Trust to bring an added $1.5 billion a year.

Said he is running for reelection to keep residents home on Maui and safe, drawing on his work as prosecutor, judge and mayor. Cited the north-south collector road and housing projects including Kilohana Mākaʻi. Said housing has increased 190% during his term, with 2,000 homes, 880 of them affordable, and that the county has a world-class emergency preparedness program.

Said she arrived on Maui in 1990, lives in Lahaina and is running because she sees nothing being done for people losing businesses and leaving the island. Said the county needs an administration that spends money and does the work rather than plans and studies. Cited her Homes Together plan for affordable housing and her Cost Cutter plan.

Said he retired in 1993 after 20 years with the SEAL Teams. Invited Kīhei residents to walk problem areas with him so he can document flood remediation ideas and pass them to whoever is mayor. Proposed a youth council where young people take part in county decisions, and said he will keep working for the people and the ʻāina.

questions.question: Many local families and workers are being priced out of Maui; what is one specific action you would take to make housing more affordable for residents?

answers.summary: Said he would go into the budget to see what the county controls rather than promise a plan off the top of his head. Said housing decisions should be put in local people's hands and urged residents to attend council meetings and vote, noting 50,000 or more people do not vote.

Said enforcing the law means ending the illegal occupation, which he said would solve housing because 300 million people can move here. Proposed working his first two years to bring a measure to the 2028 ballot. Said limited government is freedom and that the housing crisis is engineered by people who get money from developers.

Proposed a rent stabilization law and commission where residents and homeowners set maximum rents by area, with penalties or rent reductions for landlord violations, as in New York. Said 45% of residents were rent burdened in 2025 statistics. Said it would first target new rentals, with others grandfathered for a period.

questions.question: Why do you want to be mayor?

answers.summary: Said he would rather not be mayor but no one else is addressing the issue. Said he is the only candidate who accepts zero donations and that other candidates are funded by developers.

Said she worked as a scale house worker in the center of the burn zone cleanup, calculating how much they took away on trucks when they tore down homes and businesses. Said she felt more could have been done to prevent the fire and more should be done now.

Said he has put 13 years of work into the island and wants the community to work together all the time, not only after disasters. Wants to hold people accountable and get small wins like trash cans along streets, citing how people worked together after the fires.

questions.question: Traffic congestion in South Maui affects nearly everyone, from the choke point on Pi’ilani Highway to the tourist crawl on South Kīhei Road; what steps would you take to improve north-south mobility in South Maui?

answers.summary: Proposed more public transit, including trams and better, preferably free, buses that reach everyday destinations. Opposes expanding the highway, saying mainland examples show it does not help and more pavement makes cities hotter.

Said he redesigned the Maui bus system, saving about 40% in average time per line, drawing on work as a train dispatcher in Switzerland. Said an independent Hawaiʻi could regulate its borders and shift to luxury tourism and international trade, needing no new development. Said developers and officials profit from building.

Said the county is reactive, citing a speed bump at a roundabout that will cost $30,000 to remove. Proposed working with planning departments and an app so residents can vote on projects. Supports public transit, including buses from the airport to resorts to cut traffic.

questions.question: Residents in Kīhei face chronic flooding every year that shuts down parts of South Kīhei Road; what is one thing you would do as mayor to address it?

answers.summary: Proposed building swales, retention ponds and possibly a water treatment plant above the towns, and planting trees where dead grass now grows. Said new housing needs these water systems. Proposed helping residents catch rain and grow food, noting South Kīhei Road has flooded three times in five or six years.
Said Kīhei grew fast and that officials let developers defer building sewers and sidewalks, so money meant for the community was not collected. Proposed ending those deferrals for developers.

Proposed water bunds, or earth smiles, about 5 feet wide on dry slopes above Kīhei to soak water into hydrophobic soil, as used in Kenya and Tanzania. Said this would reduce flooding, runoff to the ocean and wildfire risk. Also proposed watersheds closer to the mountain.

questions.question: Bill 9 is legislation that turns thousands of short-term rentals into long-term rentals; are you for it and why, or if against it, what major step would you take to create more affordable housing in Maui?

answers.summary: Said Bill 9 gave him hope but has been divisive. Proposed buying units and hotel rooms to bring home people born here and to recruit refugee medical professionals. Said he wrote a bill guaranteeing emergency shelter or a stipend, and that housing should be treated as a right, not a commodity.

Said she voted against Bill 9, which converts about 6,000 Minatoya list units, in committee and on first and second reading, because we should build homes and not take homes from people. Proposed a system like Lima Ola using government property, infrastructure, and public private partnerships with builders. Said about 4,500 units may keep their use if the zoning change passes.

Said the American system is not working and the first step is to give the land back to Native Hawaiians, which he said would solve many problems including housing. Said Hawaiians can build and solve problems without American help, and he does not want votes from people who do not accept giving the land back.

questions.question: What is one idea or approach that you believe sets you apart from the other candidates?

answers.summary: Said they strongly believe in the strength of community, citing work in the office of economic development to help revitalize Wuku town by first finding what the community wanted. Cited the theater, the Market Street beautification plan and the municipal parking lot, with federal funding secured through a senator. Said government is only one small piece of the puzzle.

Said he has lived on three continents and embraces all cultures, but people cannot take land and occupy it. Said he saw happy people in Haiti and Africa despite little food or electricity, and that Hawaiians want to lead, be respected and be cared for, not to kick people out.

Said his background in closed ecological life support systems matches the ahupuaʻa system and could bridge traditional knowledge with science. Proposed an act raising taxes on ultra-high-value real estate and zeroing out taxes on lands with managed watersheds, so land cannot be lost to tax burdens.

questions.question: Central and South Maui share a water system at 98% capacity, South Maui has been on water restrictions for over a year and thousands of new homes are planned; what is one thing you would do to address the shortage, end restrictions and ensure smart development?

answers.summary: Said the indigenous people, the Hawaiians, know where the natural flow goes and don't need any of this technology, and that he has to consult with his family, his ʻohana, about this.

Proposed water reuse, saying South Maui has a very significant amount of water that can be recovered but it must be disinfected first. Said a systems-level mass balance analysis is needed so sustainable development fits together. Said Dory Yuki is the only council member who has never voted for sanitation.

Said South Maui's water comes from the Central Maui system, which must be protected. Supports using R-1 water to save drinkable water. Said future housing projects must come with smart meters and smart planning because water cannot be taken for granted.

questions.question: What is one reform you believe Maui County urgently needs, and how would you begin to implement it in your first year?

answers.summary: Proposed selling Maui as the best investment ever and passing a bill, which he calls MLAST on livingmaui.org, to open a pathway for wealthy people in his network to invest. Suggested about 100 grants of $1.5 million per year for 10 years, transferring potential wealth into real wealth.
Proposed amending Maui County Code chapter 2.96 to encourage employers to build housing for their workforce. Said people leave because they cannot find reasonable housing.

Said he is not interested in talking about money and spent 35 years as a stay-at-home father raising children and grandchildren. Said the reform he wants is reviving the ʻohana and aloha spirit, teaching children to love one another.

questions.question: Houselessness affects families, businesses and public spaces across Maui; what is one concrete action you would take to further address it?

answers.summary: Said every resident deserves a place to sleep at night and clean streets, parks and public spaces. Said the county works with nonprofits such as Catholic Charities and Aloha House and is rebuilding Kahalakiola in Lahina as a resource center, to create spaces where people can be housed.

Proposed her Homes Together plan, using $65 million a year in short-term rental property taxes tied to Bill 9 to give first-time buyers up to $80,000, or $110,000 with other funds, for 450 to 600 people a year, plus rental gap aid. Said a $2,700 two-bedroom needs $108,000 income. Cited U-HERO estimates of 1,900 to 3,800 lost jobs and $900 million in visitor spending.

Proposed a central county facility housing tools, equipment and materials to build prefabricated, hurricane-proof homes, which he said his research shows would speed building by 50%. Said he was told a union rejected the idea. Said it would create jobs, train young people and could serve other islands.

questions.question: After the tsunami warning, people waited two to three hours to leave South Maui on basically one exit route; if elected, is there a project you would undertake to give South Maui another form of egress?

answers.summary: Said the collector road must be finished and that planning changed a requirement for developers to build their portions into only encouraging it. Said no further development should happen until developers finish their portions. Said the first bid is due in 2027 with completion by 2030, which she said is too long to wait.

Said families and condominiums need their own emergency plans and escape routes. Proposed county vans and vehicles on call for evacuations, a hands-on county response, and a team of young people on motorcycles to help people out. Said he would be at the site of any flood or fire.

Said the North South Collector Road is moving forward and that Pani Highway speed bumps are a state project. Urged residents to sign up for the Genesis Protect app, which sets the island in grids so people evacuate at the rate asked. Said people already in a safe place should stay and not stop for gas.

questions.question: Stormwater runoff and wastewater pollution are major contributors to the decline of Maui's reefs; as mayor, what is one action you would take to reduce those impacts?

answers.summary: Proposed reservoirs on the mountainside, possibly created with shaped explosives, to collect runoff, citing Singapore. Also mentioned desalination and storing equipment in Kīhei for storms. Repeated his offer to walk flood sites with residents and give the findings to the county.

Said the county's One Water approach in Lahaina, treating stormwater and wastewater as one asset, is being considered for Kīhei. Said the county works with a Kīhei watershed group on native plants and with large landowners, noting retention basins carry dam risks. Said remaining wetlands, which catch silt before the ocean, must be kept.

Said wetlands should never be built on and Kīhei was built without hydrologists. Proposed storage facilities and a delivery system to keep storm water out of the ocean, and fixing unfinished basins to prevent silt runoff and deaths like that of a firefighter. Said it can be done with will.

questions.question: The state installed raised crosswalks at the Pi’ilani Highway roundabout and is required to fund an overpass or underpass that has not happened; how would you deal with the state on this traffic and student safety issue?

answers.summary: Said he opened Kūlanihākoʻi High School in 2023 despite a Land Use Commission ruling requiring an overpass, under a compromise banning student crossings and requiring drop-offs. Said no other Hawaiʻi high school has a required highway overpass, which would cost $14 million. Said he agreed with the DOE so the school was not wasted, and it held its first graduation last month.
